In the waiting room of the children's clinic in Aizawl, Lalremsiami sat with the baby asleep on her shoulder and dark circles under her eyes.
Disha, the clinic nurse, sat next to her while they waited. "How are nights?"
"Our plan was that I'd do all the nights, since I'm on leave and my husband, Mapuia, works. It seemed fair on paper."
"And now?"
"One month in, I'm so tired I cried over a spilled cup of tea."
Disha nodded. "That happens a lot. What does Mapuia say?"
"We talked last night. We're changing it. He'll take alternate nights. And his cousin knows a woman who helps part-time in the mornings."
"That sounds wise. And keep asking each other how you're coping, not just the baby."
"And if I keep feeling this low?"
"Then tell the doctor at your check-up. That's what we're here for."

qa.q: How was Lalremsiami feeling after the first month of doing all the nights?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was exhausted and low, so tired she cried over a spilled cup of tea.

qa.q: What else could Lalremsiami and Mapuia do to keep the new plan working?
qa.a: They could set a regular time each week to ask each other how they're coping and adjust nights or help as needed.

qa.q: How might Mapuia be affected by the change?
qa.a: Mapuia takes on alternate nights, so he will be more tired at work but more involved and able to support Lalremsiami.

grounding: It shows a couple finding after the first month that the mother handling all nights is exhausting, switching to alternate nights and part-time help, and checking how each copes.

passage:
Dear Chandrika,

Thank you for the little socks. Zoe wears them every day.
You asked how we're doing. Honestly, the first month nearly broke me. Our plan was that I'd do every night feed, since I'm on leave and Arif goes back to the bank. It made sense on paper.
By week four I was falling asleep standing at the stove. I snapped at Arif for breathing too loudly. He found me crying in the bathroom one night and said, "This plan isn't working. We change it."
Now we alternate nights. On my off-nights I sleep in the other room with earplugs. We also found an aunty from our building who comes three mornings a week so I can nap.
And every Sunday we ask each other: "How are you actually doing?" Not the baby. Us.
I feel human again, mostly.

Love,
Sabina

qa.q: How many mornings a week does the aunty from the building come?
How did Sabina feel by week four?
qa.a: Sabina felt exhausted and overwhelmed, falling asleep standing at the stove and crying in the bathroom.

qa.q: What else could Sabina and Arif do if the tiredness keeps going?
qa.a: They could mention it to the doctor at the next check-up and look for more help from family or friends.

qa.q: How might Arif have felt finding Sabina crying in the bathroom?
qa.a: Arif was probably worried and upset, realising the original plan was hurting Sabina and deciding they had to change it.

grounding: It shows a couple finding the mother-handles-nights plan exhausting after the first month, switching to alternate nights with part-time help and checking how each is coping.
